sections.text:
A Noisier World for Wildlife

A. For most of the history of life on Earth, the loudest sounds were natural ones: thunder, waves, the calls of other animals. Today, the hum of roads, the roar of aircraft and the throb of ship engines reach places that were once almost silent. Because noise leaves no visible trace, it was long treated as a nuisance for people rather than as a form of pollution affecting nature. Yet for a great many animals, hearing is not a minor sense. Birds use song to defend territories and attract partners, bats and dolphins find food by listening to echoes, and many prey species depend on detecting the faint rustle of an approaching predator. When human sound drowns out these signals, the consequences can reach far beyond simple annoyance.

B. Some of the clearest evidence comes from cities. Researchers have found that several bird species living near busy roads sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in quieter areas, lifting their songs above the low rumble of traffic. Others simply sing more loudly, a response also seen in humans, who raise their voices in a crowded restaurant without thinking about it. In some cities, robins have been recorded singing at night, when the streets are calmer. These adjustments show that birds can be remarkably flexible, but flexibility is not the same as being unaffected. A higher or louder song may demand more energy, and it may not carry the same information to a listening female as the song it replaced.

C. Studies like these face a basic problem. A noisy street is also a brightly lit, polluted and heavily built-up one, so it is hard to know whether noise itself is responsible for what scientists observe. To get around this, the field biologist Ottilie Nakamura designed an experiment in a remote woodland with no roads nearby. She placed weatherproof loudspeakers among a group of nest boxes and played recordings of traffic for part of each breeding season, leaving a similar group of boxes undisturbed for comparison. Because the woods were otherwise identical, any difference could be linked to sound alone. In her study, parents nesting near the speakers made fewer feeding visits to their young, apparently spending more time scanning for danger they could no longer hear, and their chicks left the nest at a lower weight. Nakamura is careful to describe the result as a single study of one species, but she argues that the method itself is what matters: it allows noise to be switched on and off like a variable in a laboratory.

D. Beneath the sea, the problem takes a different form. Sound travels much faster and farther in water than in air, which is why many marine animals rely on it more than on sight. Large whales produce low-frequency calls that can be detected across great distances, but the engines and propellers of cargo ships produce noise in much the same frequency range. As a result, the area over which two whales can hear each other may shrink dramatically when a vessel passes, an effect known as masking. There are signs that the noise causes stress as well. On one occasion when shipping in a busy bay was briefly interrupted, researchers found that levels of stress-related hormones in the droppings of local whales fell noticeably compared with previous years.

E. Studying animals that may be hundreds of kilometres away and rarely come to the surface requires patience and technology. The marine acoustician Bayo Lindgren fixed a line of underwater microphones, or hydrophones, to the seabed alongside a major shipping lane and left them recording for eighteen months. No team could listen to so much sound, so he trained computer software to pick out whale calls automatically and then matched them against public records of ship movements. His analysis suggested that whales calling while a large ship was nearby repeated their calls more often, as if trying to make sure they were heard. Lindgren points out, however, that hydrophones only record the animals that call; a whale that falls silent in response to noise is invisible to his equipment, so the true effect may be larger than his data show.

F. Unlike many pollutants, noise has one encouraging feature: it disappears almost as soon as its source is removed. Chemicals can remain in soil and water for decades, but a quiet road is quiet immediately. This means that practical measures can bring rapid benefits. Ships that reduce their speed in sensitive areas produce considerably less underwater noise, and newer propeller designs can make them quieter still. On land, low-noise road surfaces and barriers can reduce disturbance, and construction work can be scheduled to avoid the breeding season. The ecologist Catalina Rourke believes the most important change is a simpler one: recording the natural sounds of a site before any building begins, so that planners know what they stand to lose. As she notes, the quieter places that result are rarely appreciated by wildlife alone.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: for a great many animals, hearing is not a minor sense

explanation.en: Paragraph A explains how animals depend on sound and how human noise now reaches once-silent places. It introduces the whole problem rather than one example.
explanation.ru: Абзац A объясняет, как животные зависят от звука и как шум, создаваемый человеком, теперь доходит до мест, где раньше царила тишина. Он вводит проблему в целом, а не приводит один пример.
explanation.uk: Абзац A пояснює, як тварини залежать від звуку і як шум, створений людиною, тепер сягає місць, де колись панувала тиша. Він представляє проблему загалом, а не наводить один приклад.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in quieter areas

explanation.en: Paragraph B describes birds singing higher, louder or at night to be heard over traffic. It does not say any species benefits from noise, and it reports no disagreement among researchers.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B описано, как птицы поют выше, громче или ночью, чтобы их было слышно сквозь шум транспорта. Там не говорится, что какой-либо вид выигрывает от шума, и не упоминаются разногласия между исследователями.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B описано, як птахи співають вище, гучніше або вночі, щоб їх було чути крізь шум транспорту. Там не сказано, що якийсь вид виграє від шуму, і не згадано про розбіжності між дослідниками.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Because the woods were otherwise identical, any difference could be linked to sound alone.

explanation.en: Paragraph C is about Nakamura's experiment, which separates the effect of noise from light, pollution and buildings. Its main point is the method that tests noise alone.
explanation.ru: Абзац C посвящён эксперименту Nakamura, который отделяет влияние шума от влияния освещения, загрязнения и застройки. Главное в нём — метод, позволяющий проверить действие одного только шума.
explanation.uk: Абзац C присвячено експерименту Nakamura, який відокремлює вплив шуму від впливу освітлення, забруднення та забудови. Головне в ньому — метод, що дає змогу перевірити дію самого лише шуму.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Sound travels much faster and farther in water than in air

explanation.en: Paragraph D explains how sound travels in water and how ship noise overlaps with whale calls, causing masking and stress. It is about the problem at sea, not a research method.
explanation.ru: Абзац D объясняет, как звук распространяется в воде и как шум судов накладывается на сигналы китов, вызывая маскировку и стресс. Речь идёт о проблеме в море, а не о методе исследования.
explanation.uk: Абзац D пояснює, як звук поширюється у воді і як шум суден накладається на сигнали китів, спричиняючи маскування та стрес. Ідеться про проблему в морі, а не про метод дослідження.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: left them recording for eighteen months

explanation.en: Paragraph E describes Lindgren's hydrophones recording beside a shipping lane and what they showed about whale calls when ships were nearby.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E описаны гидрофоны Lindgren, которые вели запись рядом с судоходным путём, и то, что они показали о сигналах китов, когда поблизости проходили суда.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E описано гідрофони Lindgren, які записували звук поруч із судноплавним шляхом, і те, що вони показали щодо сигналів китів, коли поблизу проходили судна.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: it disappears almost as soon as its source is removed

explanation.en: Paragraph F stresses that noise, unlike chemicals, stops quickly, so practical measures work fast. Laws are not mentioned, so the heading about new laws is wrong.
explanation.ru: Абзац F подчёркивает, что шум, в отличие от химических веществ, быстро прекращается, поэтому практические меры дают результат сразу. Законы не упоминаются, так что заголовок о новых законах не подходит.
explanation.uk: Абзац F наголошує, що шум, на відміну від хімічних речовин, швидко зникає, тож практичні заходи дають результат одразу. Закони не згадуються, тому заголовок про нові закони не підходить.

explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что зафиксированные сигналы китов сопоставляли с открытыми данными о передвижении судов.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що зафіксовані сигнали китів зіставляли з відкритими даними про рух суден.

sections.text:
From Scribe to Press: How Printing Changed Reading

A. Before the middle of the fifteenth century, every book in Europe had to be copied by hand. Professional scribes, many of them working in monasteries and later in commercial workshops attached to universities, could spend months producing a single volume. The materials added to the cost: much writing was done on parchment, prepared from animal skins, and a large book might require the skins of well over a hundred animals. As a result, books were valuable possessions, often chained to desks in libraries or listed alongside land and jewellery in wills. Copying also introduced mistakes. Each scribe worked from an earlier copy, so a careless slip could be passed down and multiplied, and two manuscripts of the same work rarely matched word for word. Readers who wanted to compare texts faced a genuine problem: they could not be sure they were reading the same words.

B. The change began in the German city of Mainz around 1450. What emerged there was less a single invention than a clever assembly of existing techniques. Metalworkers already knew how to cast objects in moulds; presses with a large screw were used to squeeze grapes and olives; and paper, which had reached Europe centuries earlier from the Islamic world, had become far cheaper than parchment. The decisive step was to cast individual letters in metal, all of identical height, so that they could be arranged into lines, locked into a frame, inked, printed and then taken apart and reused. A new oil-based ink, which clung to metal better than the water-based inks used by scribes, completed the system. A small team could now produce hundreds of identical pages in the time a scribe needed for a handful.

C. The method spread with remarkable speed. Workers trained in Mainz moved on to other cities, taking their skills with them, and by 1500 printing presses had been set up in more than two hundred towns across Europe. Venice, with its wealthy merchants and its position at the centre of trade routes, became one of the busiest centres of all. Yet printing was a risky business. A printer had to pay for metal, paper and labour long before a single copy was sold, and many early firms went bankrupt. To survive, printers chose titles they were confident would find buyers: prayer books, school grammars, calendars and legal handbooks. Far from being driven only by scholarly ideals, the early book trade followed the market.

D. Printing also altered the appearance and reliability of the book. Because buyers could now choose among competing editions in a shop, printers added features to attract and guide them. Title pages announced the content and often the place where copies could be purchased; page numbers and indexes allowed readers to find a passage quickly and to direct others to it. Smaller formats made books portable and cheaper. At the same time, the process had a double effect on accuracy. A carefully corrected text could be reproduced exactly, so scholars in different cities could at last discuss the same page. But an error that slipped past the printer appeared in every copy of the edition. Over time, the habits of influential printers also encouraged more consistent spelling, although full standardisation came much later.

E. Whether print made more people literate is harder to establish. Literacy in this period left few direct traces, and historians must rely on indirect evidence. One study by the historian Margit Hallström examined lists of possessions drawn up after deaths in several northern European towns during the sixteenth century. She found that books, rare in the homes of craftsmen at the start of the century, appeared in a growing share of them by its end, usually as one or two cheap religious titles. Hallström cautions that owning a book did not prove that anyone in the household could read it. Reading aloud was common, so a single literate family member might share a text with others, and many people who could read had never learned to write.

F. The economic historian Rashid Kalnins argues that the press amplified a demand for reading that already existed rather than creating one from nothing. Towns were growing, merchants needed records, and religious movements urged believers to read scripture in their own languages; printing allowed these pressures to be met on a scale that copying by hand never could. In the 1520s, for example, short pamphlets in German on religious questions were printed in huge numbers and passed from hand to hand. Even so, Kalnins notes, the proportion of Europeans who could read rose slowly, and in most regions it was the gradual expansion of schooling over the following centuries that turned reading into an everyday skill. The press, in his view, was a necessary condition for mass literacy but not a sufficient one.

questions.prompt: Paragraph A
questions.evidence: Professional scribes, many of them working in monasteries and later in commercial workshops attached to universities, could spend months producing a single volume.

explanation.en: Paragraph A describes how hand copying took months, used expensive parchment and introduced mistakes. Scribes are mentioned, but nothing is said about them resisting printing.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A описано, как переписывание от руки занимало месяцы, требовало дорогого пергамента и порождало ошибки. Переписчики упоминаются, но ничего не сказано о том, что они сопротивлялись книгопечатанию.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A описано, як переписування від руки тривало місяцями, потребувало дорогого пергаменту й породжувало помилки. Переписувачів згадано, але нічого не сказано про те, що вони опиралися книгодрукуванню.

questions.prompt: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: What emerged there was less a single invention than a clever assembly of existing techniques.

explanation.en: Paragraph B explains that printing combined casting, screw presses, paper and new ink. Cheap paper is only one part of this, so the heading about paper replacing parchment is too narrow.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B объясняется, что книгопечатание объединило литьё литер, винтовой пресс, бумагу и новую краску. Дешёвая бумага — лишь одна из этих составляющих, поэтому заголовок о том, что бумага вытеснила пергамент, слишком узкий.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B пояснено, що книгодрукування поєднало лиття літер, гвинтовий прес, папір і нову фарбу. Дешевий папір — лише одна з цих складових, тому заголовок про те, що папір витіснив пергамент, надто вузький.

questions.prompt: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Yet printing was a risky business.

explanation.en: Paragraph C describes how fast printing spread and how the risk of losing money made printers choose titles that would sell.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C описано, как быстро распространялось книгопечатание и как риск потерять деньги заставлял печатников выбирать книги, которые будут хорошо продаваться.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C описано, як швидко поширювалося книгодрукування і як ризик втратити гроші змушував друкарів обирати книжки, що добре продаватимуться.

questions.prompt: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Printing also altered the appearance and reliability of the book.

explanation.en: Paragraph D covers new features such as title pages and indexes, and the double effect of printing on accuracy.
explanation.ru: Абзац D посвящён новшествам, таким как титульные листы и указатели, а также двоякому влиянию книгопечатания на точность текстов.
explanation.uk: Абзац D присвячено новаціям, як-от титульні аркуші та покажчики, а також подвійному впливу книгодрукування на точність текстів.

questions.prompt: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: Literacy in this period left few direct traces, and historians must rely on indirect evidence.

explanation.en: Paragraph E reports a study of lists of possessions showing books appearing in craftsmen's homes, while warning that owning a book did not prove anyone could read it.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E говорится об исследовании описей имущества, которое показывает, что книги появлялись в домах ремесленников, но с оговоркой: владение книгой ещё не доказывало, что кто-то мог её прочитать.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E йдеться про дослідження описів майна, яке показує, що книжки з'являлися в оселях ремісників, але із застереженням: володіння книжкою ще не доводило, що хтось умів її прочитати.

questions.prompt: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: the press amplified a demand for reading that already existed rather than creating one from nothing

explanation.en: Paragraph F presents the view that printing strengthened an existing demand for reading but did not on its own create mass literacy.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F изложена точка зрения, что книгопечатание усилило уже существовавший спрос на чтение, но само по себе не привело к массовой грамотности.
explanation.uk: В абзаці F викладено думку, що книгодрукування посилило вже наявний попит на читання, але саме по собі не спричинило масової грамотності.

explanation.uk: В абзаці B сказано, що всі металеві літери мали однакову висоту, тож їх можна було складати в рядки й використовувати повторно.

questions.prompt: The water-based inks of the scribes were replaced by an ______ ink that stuck to the metal type more effectively.
questions.evidence: A new oil-based ink, which clung to metal better than the water-based inks used by scribes

explanation.en: Paragraph B describes a new oil-based ink that 'clung to metal better', which the summary restates as 'stuck to the metal type more effectively'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B описана новая краска на масляной основе, которая «clung to metal better»; в кратком изложении это перефразировано как «stuck to the metal type more effectively».
explanation.uk: В абзаці B описано нову фарбу на олійній основі, яка «clung to metal better»; у підсумку це перефразовано як «stuck to the metal type more effectively».

questions.prompt: Workers trained in Mainz carried the technique elsewhere, and by 1500 presses were operating in over ______ European towns.
questions.evidence: by 1500 printing presses had been set up in more than two hundred towns across Europe

explanation.en: Paragraph C gives the figure of more than two hundred towns by 1500.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C приводится цифра: к 1500 году — более двухсот городов.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C наведено цифру: до 1500 року — понад двісті міст.

options.text: Scribes in monasteries changed passages they disagreed with.
Mistakes made by one copyist were inherited by later copies.
Parchment from different animals affected how words were written.
Universities and monasteries each preferred their own versions.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph A, why did two manuscripts of the same work often differ?
questions.evidence: Each scribe worked from an earlier copy, so a careless slip could be passed down and multiplied

explanation.en: Paragraph A says each scribe copied from an earlier copy, so errors were passed down. Monasteries, universities and parchment are mentioned, but not as reasons why texts differed.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A сказано, что каждый переписчик копировал с более ранней копии, поэтому ошибки передавались дальше. Монастыри, университеты и пергамент упоминаются, но не как причины расхождений между текстами.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A сказано, що кожен переписувач копіював з попередньої копії, тому помилки передавалися далі. Монастирі, університети й пергамент згадано, але не як причини розбіжностей між текстами.

options.text: It quickly produced a single standard spelling everywhere.
It removed mistakes because printers checked every page.
It could preserve a correct text but also repeat a fault.
It made errors far more common than in manuscripts.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the effect of printing on accuracy?
questions.evidence: A carefully corrected text could be reproduced exactly, so scholars in different cities could at last discuss the same page. But an error that slipped past the printer appeared in every copy of the edition.

explanation.en: Paragraph D describes a 'double effect': correct texts could be copied exactly, but an error appeared in every copy. The writer says full standardisation of spelling came much later, so the option about a quick single standard is wrong.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D описан «double effect»: правильные тексты можно было воспроизводить точно, но ошибка попадала в каждый экземпляр. Автор пишет, что полная стандартизация орфографии наступила гораздо позже, поэтому вариант о быстром появлении единого стандарта неверен.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D описано «double effect»: правильні тексти можна було відтворювати точно, але помилка потрапляла в кожен примірник. Автор пише, що повна стандартизація правопису настала значно пізніше, тому варіант про швидку появу єдиного стандарту хибний.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

Craftsmen bought religious books mainly to show off their wealth.
Lists of possessions often leave out cheap books owned by families.
Having a book at home does not show that anyone there could read.

questions.prompt: What warning does Margit Hallström give about her findings?
questions.evidence: Hallström cautions that owning a book did not prove that anyone in the household could read it.

explanation.en: Paragraph E says Hallström warns that owning a book did not prove anyone in the household could read. The passage says 'many people' could read but not write; it does not say this was true of most craftsmen.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что Hallström предупреждает: владение книгой не доказывало, что кто-либо в семье умел читать. В тексте говорится, что «many people» умели читать, но не писать; о том, что это относилось к большинству ремесленников, не сказано.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що Hallström застерігає: володіння книжкою не доводило, що хтось у родині вмів читати. У тексті йдеться, що «many people» вміли читати, але не писати; про те, що це стосувалося більшості ремісників, не сказано.

meta.topic: Printing and the spread of reading

sections.text:
The Trouble with Open Offices

A. Walk into almost any modern workplace and you are likely to find the same arrangement: long rows of desks, no internal walls, and managers seated, at least in theory, among their staff. The open-plan office has become so familiar that it is easy to forget it was once a radical idea. Its roots lie partly in a German movement of the late 1950s known as Bürolandschaft, or 'office landscape', which grouped desks organically to reflect how information actually flowed between teams. Today's version, however, owes less to that philosophy than to accountancy. Removing walls allows more employees to fit into less floor space, and the savings on rent can be considerable. Supporters rarely lead with this argument. Instead, they claim that openness encourages conversation, speeds up decisions and breaks down hierarchy. It is these claims, rather than the financial ones, that deserve scrutiny.

B. The central promise is that people who can see one another will talk more. When the organisational researcher Henrik Abalos tracked two firms as they moved from cellular offices into open floors, he found the reverse. Using wearable sensors that recorded when colleagues were within speaking distance, his team observed that face-to-face exchanges fell by roughly two-thirds in the months after the move, while emails and instant messages rose sharply. Abalos's explanation is that people who feel constantly observed seek privacy in whatever way they can: they wear headphones, avoid eye contact and move conversations onto screens. "Remove the walls," he says, "and employees build invisible ones." His study involved only two companies, and he is careful not to generalise too widely, but the pattern is difficult to dismiss.

C. Noise is the most obvious complaint, and also the most misunderstood. Yasmin Thorvald, an acoustics engineer who advises companies on office design, points out that overall volume is rarely the real problem. A steady background hum, such as the sound of ventilation, can actually help concentration. What damages it is intelligible speech: a conversation at the next desk that the brain cannot help following. Thorvald's measurements suggest that a single nearby phone call can be more disruptive than the general noise of a busy café. Carpets and ceiling panels reduce echo, she says, but they cannot stop words from carrying across a few metres of open floor. Her advice to clients is therefore less about absorbing sound than about separating people who need to talk from people who need to think.

D. Distraction has consequences beyond irritation. The environmental psychologist Mercedes Okonjo asked 240 volunteers to complete demanding writing and checking tasks in either a quiet room or a simulated open office. Those in the open setting made more errors on average. More surprisingly, they also reported greater fatigue at the end of the session, including participants whose scores were no worse than those of the quiet group. Okonjo argues that the effort of filtering out unwanted sound is itself tiring, so its cost may be hidden from managers who look only at output. Her volunteers worked on set tasks for a single afternoon, so the effects over months remain unknown. Those who described themselves as easily distracted suffered most, which suggests that a single layout cannot suit everyone equally.

E. None of this means that walls should simply return. Defenders of open plans are right that private offices can isolate people and reinforce status; few would wish to revive the corridor of closed doors with the most senior names on the largest rooms. Nor is collaboration a myth. Some work genuinely benefits from overheard conversation: a junior employee who catches a colleague solving a problem may learn more than any training course could teach. The difficulty is that most office work alternates between such moments and long stretches of solitary concentration, and the standard open floor caters for only one of them.

F. The more promising approach, in my view, is to give employees a choice of settings. Some organisations have experimented with what is often called activity-based working, in which staff move between quiet zones, small enclosed booths for phone calls, and open areas for group work. Okonjo is cautiously supportive of such designs, but she warns that they fail when the quiet spaces are too few or when people feel they must remain visible at their desks to be seen as hard-working. Tariq Mendelsohn, a facilities manager who oversaw one such redesign, found that the booths were booked solid within a week, while a quarter of the open desks sat empty. The lesson he drew was that the company had underestimated the demand for quiet, not that the design had failed.

G. The question, then, is not whether open-plan offices work, but what they are being asked to do. If the aim is to cut costs, they succeed. If the aim is to make people collaborate, the evidence suggests that removing walls is a blunt and sometimes counterproductive tool. Collaboration depends on trust, shared goals and time, none of which can be delivered by a floor plan. Managers who knock down walls in the hope of creating a lively, creative atmosphere are, in effect, asking furniture to do the work of leadership. Organisations that want both conversation and concentration will need to design for both, and accept that the cheapest layout is rarely the most productive one.
sections.title: The Trouble with Open Offices

questions.prompt: Saving money, rather than the original design philosophy, explains the spread of today's open-plan offices.
questions.evidence: Today's version, however, owes less to that philosophy than to accountancy.

explanation.en: In Paragraph A the writer says modern open offices come more from 'accountancy' (saving money on rent) than from the ideas of the Bürolandschaft movement. This matches the statement.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A автор пишет, что современные открытые офисы появились скорее из соображений "accountancy" (экономии на аренде), чем из идей движения Bürolandschaft. Это совпадает с утверждением.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A автор пише, що сучасні відкриті офіси з'явилися радше з міркувань "accountancy" (економії на оренді), ніж з ідей руху Bürolandschaft. Це збігається з твердженням.

questions.prompt: People who promote open-plan offices usually begin by pointing to the money they save.
questions.evidence: Supporters rarely lead with this argument.

explanation.en: In Paragraph A the writer says supporters 'rarely lead with' the financial argument and talk about conversation and hierarchy instead. This is the opposite of the statement.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A автор говорит, что сторонники "rarely lead with" финансовый аргумент, а вместо этого говорят об общении и иерархии. Это противоположно утверждению.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A автор каже, що прихильники "rarely lead with" фінансовий аргумент, а натомість говорять про спілкування та ієрархію. Це протилежне твердженню.

questions.prompt: Wearing headphones is an effective way for workers to reduce distraction in an open-plan office.

explanation.en: Paragraph B mentions headphones only as one way people try to get privacy. The writer never says whether headphones actually reduce distraction, so the writer's view cannot be known.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B наушники упоминаются лишь как один из способов, которыми люди пытаются уединиться. Автор нигде не говорит, действительно ли наушники уменьшают отвлечение, поэтому его мнение узнать нельзя.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B навушники згадано лише як один зі способів, якими люди намагаються усамітнитися. Автор ніде не каже, чи справді навушники зменшують відволікання, тож його думку дізнатися неможливо.

questions.prompt: Abalos's results deserve attention even though his study was limited in size.
questions.evidence: His study involved only two companies, and he is careful not to generalise too widely, but the pattern is difficult to dismiss.

explanation.en: In Paragraph B the writer admits the study covered only two companies but says the pattern is 'difficult to dismiss', meaning it should be taken seriously.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B автор признаёт, что исследование охватило только две компании, но называет закономерность "difficult to dismiss" — то есть к ней стоит отнестись серьёзно.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B автор визнає, що дослідження охопило лише дві компанії, але називає закономірність "difficult to dismiss" — тобто до неї варто поставитися серйозно.

questions.prompt: Okonjo's experiment should have included a larger number of participants.

explanation.en: Paragraph D gives the number of volunteers (240) and points out one limitation: the tasks lasted only one afternoon. The writer says nothing about whether the group was too small.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D указано число добровольцев (240) и названо одно ограничение: задания длились всего полдня. О том, не была ли группа слишком маленькой, автор ничего не говорит.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D вказано кількість добровольців (240) і названо одне обмеження: завдання тривали лише пів дня. Про те, чи не була група замалою, автор нічого не каже.

questions.prompt: Private offices should be brought back for most employees.
questions.evidence: None of this means that walls should simply return.

explanation.en: At the start of Paragraph E the writer clearly says the problems of open offices do not mean walls should return, and adds that private offices can isolate people. This contradicts the statement.
explanation.ru: В начале абзаца E автор прямо говорит, что недостатки открытых офисов не означают, что нужно возвращать стены, и добавляет, что отдельные кабинеты могут изолировать людей. Это противоречит утверждению.
explanation.uk: На початку абзацу E автор прямо каже, що недоліки відкритих офісів не означають, що слід повертати стіни, і додає, що окремі кабінети можуть ізолювати людей. Це суперечить твердженню.

groups.instruction: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer in the passage? Write YES if the statement agrees with the views of the writer, NO if the statement contradicts the views of the writer, or NOT GIVEN if it is impossible to say what the writer thinks about this.

options.text: placing senior managers in private rooms set well apart from their staff
fitting as many employees as possible into the smallest floor space
grouping desks to mirror how information moved between teams
setting out desks in long straight rows without internal walls

questions.prompt: What was the main idea behind the Bürolandschaft movement?
questions.evidence: grouped desks organically to reflect how information actually flowed between teams

explanation.en: Paragraph A says the movement grouped desks to reflect how information flowed between teams. Fitting more people into less space describes today's offices, and long rows of desks are also part of the modern arrangement, not the 1950s idea.
explanation.ru: В абзаце A сказано, что движение группировало столы так, чтобы отразить, как информация передавалась между командами. Размещение большего числа людей на меньшей площади описывает сегодняшние офисы, а длинные ряды столов — тоже черта современной планировки, а не идея 1950-х годов.
explanation.uk: В абзаці A сказано, що рух групував столи так, щоб відобразити, як інформація передавалася між командами. Розміщення більшої кількості людей на меншій площі описує сучасні офіси, а довгі ряди столів — теж риса сучасного планування, а не ідея 1950-х років.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

options.text: Staff talked in person less but sent about the same number of emails.
Staff talked in person more at first but less after some months.
Staff talked in person more and sent fewer written messages.
Staff talked in person less and communicated more through screens.

questions.prompt: What did Abalos find after the two firms moved into open floors?
questions.evidence: face-to-face exchanges fell by roughly two-thirds in the months after the move, while emails and instant messages rose sharply

explanation.en: Paragraph B says face-to-face exchanges fell while emails and instant messages rose sharply. The emails did not stay the same, and there was no early increase in conversation.
explanation.ru: В абзаце B говорится, что личного общения стало меньше, а число писем и мгновенных сообщений резко выросло. Количество писем не осталось прежним, и никакого первоначального роста общения не было.
explanation.uk: В абзаці B йдеться про те, що особистого спілкування поменшало, а кількість листів і миттєвих повідомлень різко зросла. Кількість листів не залишилася такою самою, і жодного початкового зростання спілкування не було.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

options.text: speech that listeners can make out and follow
echoes created by hard floors and bare ceiling surfaces
a high overall level of sound across the whole office
the constant background hum of ventilation systems

questions.prompt: According to Thorvald, what does the most harm to concentration?
questions.evidence: What damages it is intelligible speech: a conversation at the next desk that the brain cannot help following.

explanation.en: Paragraph C says the problem is 'intelligible speech' that the brain cannot help following. Thorvald says overall volume is rarely the problem, and a steady hum can actually help concentration.
explanation.ru: В абзаце C сказано, что проблема — это "intelligible speech", за которой мозг не может не следить. Thorvald говорит, что общая громкость редко бывает проблемой, а ровный фоновый гул может даже помогать сосредоточиться.
explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що проблема — це "intelligible speech", за якою мозок не може не стежити. Thorvald каже, що загальна гучність рідко буває проблемою, а рівний фоновий гул може навіть допомагати зосередитися.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

options.text: Workers in the quiet room reported more tiredness than those in the open office.
Open-setting workers felt more tired even when they scored equally well.
Workers in the open setting made fewer errors than the researchers expected.
Workers who were easily distracted actually did better in the open setting.

questions.prompt: What was surprising about Okonjo's findings?
questions.evidence: they also reported greater fatigue at the end of the session, including participants whose scores were no worse than those of the quiet group

explanation.en: Paragraph D calls it 'more surprising' that people in the open setting felt more tired, even those whose scores were as good as the quiet group's. Easily distracted workers suffered most, not least, and the open group made more errors, not fewer.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D автор называет "more surprising" то, что люди в открытом пространстве уставали сильнее — даже те, чьи результаты были не хуже, чем у группы в тишине. Сильнее всего страдали как раз легко отвлекающиеся сотрудники, а не наоборот, и группа в открытом пространстве делала больше ошибок, а не меньше.
explanation.uk: В абзаці D автор називає "more surprising" те, що люди у відкритому просторі втомлювалися більше — навіть ті, чиї результати були не гірші, ніж у групи в тиші. Найбільше страждали саме працівники, які легко відволікаються, а не навпаки, і група у відкритому просторі робила більше помилок, а не менше.

groups.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

questions.prompt: Okonjo believes that ______ unwanted noise is in itself an exhausting effort for workers.
questions.evidence: Okonjo argues that the effort of filtering out unwanted sound is itself tiring

explanation.en: Paragraph D says the effort of 'filtering out' unwanted sound is tiring. 'Exhausting' in the summary restates 'tiring'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сказано, что усилия, необходимые для "filtering out" ненужных звуков, утомляют ("tiring"). Слово "exhausting" в кратком изложении перефразирует "tiring".
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що зусилля, потрібні для "filtering out" непотрібних звуків, втомлюють ("tiring"). Слово "exhausting" у короткому викладі перефразовує "tiring".

questions.prompt: Because this cost is hidden, managers who pay attention only to ______ may fail to notice it.
questions.evidence: its cost may be hidden from managers who look only at output

explanation.en: Paragraph D says the cost may be hidden from managers who 'look only at output'. 'Pay attention only to' restates 'look only at'.
explanation.ru: В абзаце D сказано, что эти потери могут оставаться незаметными для руководителей, которые "look only at output". Выражение "pay attention only to" в кратком изложении перефразирует "look only at".
explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що ці втрати можуть лишатися непомітними для керівників, які "look only at output". Вираз "pay attention only to" у короткому викладі перефразовує "look only at".

questions.prompt: The writer accepts that a junior employee may learn more from ______ than from any formal training.
questions.evidence: Some work genuinely benefits from overheard conversation

explanation.en: Paragraph E says some work benefits from 'overheard conversation', giving the example of a junior employee who learns by catching a colleague solving a problem.
explanation.ru: В абзаце E сказано, что некоторым видам работы идёт на пользу "overheard conversation", и приводится пример младшего сотрудника, который учится, случайно услышав, как коллега решает задачу.
explanation.uk: В абзаці E сказано, що деяким видам роботи йде на користь "overheard conversation", і наведено приклад молодшого працівника, який навчається, випадково почувши, як колега розв'язує проблему.

questions.prompt: In activity-based working, staff can use small enclosed ______ when they need to make phone calls.
questions.evidence: small enclosed booths for phone calls

explanation.en: Paragraph F lists 'small enclosed booths for phone calls' as one of the spaces in activity-based working.
explanation.ru: В абзаце F "small enclosed booths for phone calls" названы одним из типов пространств в модели "activity-based working".
explanation.uk: В абзаці F "small enclosed booths for phone calls" названо одним із типів просторів у моделі "activity-based working".

groups.instruction: Complete the summary below. Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.
